nodes.subject: Matias community discussion
nodes.object: one board at 70, 160, and 170 dollar price points, quiet office use, feel disagreement, and heavy-use durability concerns

support_spans.exact_quote: Found this on eBay, new in box for $70.00. Matias sells these for $170 new and Amazon has them for $160.
Matias Quiet Click switches are VERY quiet. If you're going to use them in an office, nobody would care.

You got yourself an ace bargain. I am envious and and thrilled. I have gone through two Matias boards as my daily drivers. I found that they don't hold up well to 10 hours a day, 5 days a week. The switches go after a couple of years. Enjoy.

accepted_phrases: The Matias thread reports 70, 160, and 170 dollar prices for one model, quiet office use, and a participant's heavy-use durability concern; these are community experiences, not stable prices or failure rates.

nodes.subject: silent-switch community comparison
nodes.object: the cheapest tested option was reported quietest, another had the best tactile feel, and plate and case affect remaining sound

support_spans.exact_quote: Outemu Silent Peach/Lime : would you have guessed that the cheapest switches on this list are the quietest?
BEST FEEL Gazzew U4 Boba : if you're looking for a silent tactile and want the best tactility, I think this is definitely king.
But the plate material and case have a lot to say what happens to the sound that is left.

accepted_phrases: The silent-switch thread separates quietness from tactile feel: the author reports the cheapest tested option as quietest, a different option as best-feeling, and a commenter says plate material and case shape residual sound; this is anecdotal, not a controlled ranking.

nodes.subject: Gamakay budget daily-driver review
nodes.object: quiet daily use and acceptable lube with cheaper-feeling housing, flimsy pins, and installation difficulty

support_spans.exact_quote: In terms of build quality, the switches feel pretty decent, with adequate factory lube and no semblance of stemrattle whatsoever. The plastic housing, however, does seem a little bit cheap when compared to other switches like the Gaetron Reds.
My biggest issue with the switches were the metal pins.

I would personally recommend the Gamakay Pheonix for a budget build that's to be used by someone needing a great typing experience without worrying about disturbing others while hacking away at their keys.

accepted_phrases: The Gamakay review reports a quiet budget daily-driver result and adequate factory lube, while also reporting cheaper-feeling housing, flimsy pins, and installation difficulty; it is one user's scoped review.

nodes.subject: NiZ community discussion
nodes.object: switches, lubricant, stabilizers, plates, and foams were tried before one out-of-box board was judged comparable in sound and enjoyable to type on

support_spans.exact_quote: I'd read about EC / Topre switches on here before but after buying dozens of mechanical keyboards and built a couple, trying various switches, lubes, stabs, plates, foam, tape mod, pe foam etc etc I took this out the box and it sounds just as good as a fully modded board! And the switches are a joy to type on.

accepted_phrases: The NiZ author lists switches, lubricant, stabilizers, plates, and foams among prior modification work, then reports one out-of-box board as sounding as good to that author and being enjoyable to type on; it does not establish a general ranking.

nodes.subject: typing-style and switch discussion

support_spans.exact_quote: Sound is a result of board, plate and keycaps, not the switch.
He was dead set on MX Blues for tactility, but one try of my MX Blue keyboard and the noise was not to his liking.
Tactiles felt tiring to type on for me.

accepted_phrases: The typing-style thread contains participant reports that board, plate, keycaps, and chassis shape sound and that noise or fatigue can reverse a switch preference; these are scoped opinions that motivate hands-on testing.

nodes.subject: computer keyboard layouts
nodes.object: keyboard types target different needs and tenkeyless designs commonly omit the number pad for compactness or preference

support_spans.exact_quote: Different types of keyboards are available and each is designed with a focus on specific features that suit particular needs.
The most common choice is to not include the numpad, which can usually be fully replaced by the alphanumeric section; such designs are referred to as "tenkeyless" (or TKL).

accepted_phrases: The computer-keyboard source says keyboard types target different needs and describes tenkeyless designs as commonly omitting the number pad for compactness or preference, so key count is a fit decision rather than a simple quality tier.

nodes.subject: keyboard posture and mouse reach
nodes.object: forearms parallel and wrists straight, with compact layouts freeing mouse space and reducing outward arm rotation

support_spans.exact_quote: Consideration of physical ergonomics suggests the most relaxed typing position is one in which the keyboard user's forearms are parallel to the ground, with wrists held straight.

Compact keyboards lack the numeric block which is rarely used. They are considered ergonomic [ 8 ] as it frees up space to the right side of the keyboard for better placement of the mouse. This reduces the outward rotation angle of the arm when switching to the mouse .

accepted_phrases: The ergonomic-keyboard source identifies forearms parallel to the ground and straight wrists as a relaxed posture and explains that a compact layout can free mouse space and reduce outward arm rotation; it does not make one layout universally correct.

nodes.subject: Model M construction example
nodes.object: a heavy steel backplate and strong plastic frame are associated with surviving units, while the buckling-spring design has a distinctive feel and sound

support_spans.exact_quote: Thanks to the M's design, including its heavy steel backplate and strong plastic frame, many early Model M Keyboards are still functional four decades past release.
The Model M's buckling spring key design specification [ 34 ] gives it a unique feel and sound.

accepted_phrases: The Model M source links one specific design's heavy steel backplate and strong plastic frame with surviving units and says its buckling-spring design has a distinctive feel and sound; this is an example, not proof that price or weight guarantees durability.
